finding: The system does not stay silent, and the brief's own wording anticipates this: 413 of 9,711 benign connections raise something, a false-positive rate of 4.25% -- about 1 in 24. The layers contribute 235 rule hits, 287 supervised alerts and 152 anomaly alerts (overlapping, so these sum to more than the total). The rules doing it are R06 (vertical port scan, 113), R04 (malformed ip fragmentation, 52), R10 (guest session with file activity, 43), R11 (root shell obtained, 19), and the benign populations that trigger them are exactly the ones a real network has: a monitoring system polling many hosts, a client retrying closed ports, an anonymous FTP download, an administrator using su. No threshold on these features separates them, because at connection level they are not different -- the intent is, and intent is not in the record. What the hybrid can do is rank: 232 of these land at medium or low because no second layer corroborates them, so they sort below the corroborated attacks rather than competing with them. 173 still reach critical, which is the residual cost and is stated as such.

Scanning is defined by the *spread* of a source's connections rather than their content, and diff_srv_rate, dst_host_diff_srv_rate and the rejected-connection rates measure that spread directly, so a hand-written rule and a learned tree arrive at nearly the same boundary. High recall on this class and a 4.3% benign alarm rate are the same fact measured from two sides, not two independent results.

finding: This is where the hybrid architecture earns its cost, and also where the system is weakest overall. R2L recall is 25.5% and U2R 59.7% across 21 families, and the aggregate hides which layer is doing the work. These are the rarest classes in the corpus, so the supervised layer has the least to learn from: it recovers guess_passwd 0.0%, sendmail 0.0%, snmpgetattack 0.0%. The signature layer does not care about class balance -- R09 counts failed logins, R10 flags guest sessions that create files, and R11/R12 look for root_shell, su_attempted and root-level file activity -- so on 9 of these families it is the strongest layer of the three. The largest hybrid-over-supervised gains are loadmodule +100%, sqlattack +100%, buffer_overflow +60%. The anomaly layer contributes little here (its best family here is httptunnel at 32.3%), because a brute-force login and a root shell are statistically ordinary connections; where it is 0.000 that is a null result and it is reported as one. Two honest caveats remain. First, this is not detection of the attack but of its aftermath -- a matched R11 means a root shell was already obtained. Second, the same counters fire on an administrator legitimately using su, which is part of the scenario-1 false-positive rate: the signature layer trades false alarms on benign admin activity for recall on privilege escalation. On this corpus that trade is worth making, but it is a trade, not a free improvement.

That gap of 20% is the single most important number in this evaluation, and it is the one a headline accuracy figure hides. The worst case is 'snmpguess' (r2l, 331 connections): hybrid recall 0.0%, with the signature layer at 0.0%, the supervised layer at 0.0% and the anomaly layer at 0.0%. Every layer fails for its own reason and the reasons compound rather than cancel: no rule was written for behaviour nobody had characterised, the classifier has no decision region for a class it never saw, and the anomaly layer -- the one layer that is supposed to cover exactly this -- is silent because these connections are not statistically unusual. They are ordinary-looking sessions on ordinary services carrying a hostile payload. At connection-record granularity they are genuinely indistinguishable from benign traffic, so this is not a tuning problem: no threshold on these features separates them. Closing it needs different evidence -- payload inspection, or host-level telemetry -- not a better model over the same features.

finding: The pipeline runs unchanged on flows assembled from raw packets, which is the useful part: the same rules and the same fitted models apply to 755 flows reconstructed from the capture in 2.02s. What the capture shows is the limit of the record format rather than of the detector. No alert at all is raised for 10.0.0.50 (0/90 flows, top severity none). Rule-backed detections: 10.0.0.66 (30/30 flows, top severity critical) via R07 x27, R06 x23; 10.0.0.99 (595/595 flows, top severity critical) via R01 x495. Flagged by the learned layers with no rule behind them: 10.0.0.77 (40/40 flows, top severity low). Those are the interesting ones. They are detected, but they are detected weakly -- no signature matched, so nothing corroborates the models and the corroboration discount pushes them to the bottom of the queue. The structural reason is the record format: the dst_host_* features summarise behaviour per destination, and a sweep touches each destination once, so that history is empty at the moment each flow is scored. A scan that spreads across hosts defeats features that summarise behaviour per host, and the flow-level rules that would catch it have nothing to count. That is an argument for correlating across destinations at a level above the flow record, which this design does not do.
